threads.body: `BatchState`'s `commands`/`asyncCommands` lists (plain `ArrayList`s) and its `parentContext` field are mutated in `add()` during command dispatch and read/drained in `start()`/`drainCommands()`/`drainAsyncCommands()` during flush, all without synchronization. A Lettuce connection is thread-safe and applications may issue commands from multiple threads while auto-flush is disabled, so concurrent `add()` calls, or `add()` racing with the drain on flush, can corrupt the list state or throw `ConcurrentModificationException`. The analogous `BatchState` in the lettuce-5.1 library (`OpenTelemetryTracing.BatchState`) synchronizes its access; consider applying the same protection here (e.g. synchronize the `add`/drain methods and perform the "drain if non-empty" check atomically).

These six new methods (`setAutoFlushCommands`, `capture`, `startBatch`, `finishBatch`, `startCommand`, `endCommand`) are javaagent-only bridges, yet they are added to the public, stable `LettuceTelemetry` entrypoint. This permanently expands the library's public API surface with internal batch machinery that uses untyped `Object` parameters and an `Object` return value, which is confusing for library consumers who call `LettuceTelemetry` directly.

The established convention in this repo is to keep javaagent-shared/internal helpers in a `...v5_1.internal` package marked "This class is internal and is hence not for public use" (e.g. `io.opentelemetry.instrumentation.r2dbc.v1_0.internal.Experimental`), so they are excluded from API-stability guarantees. Consider moving these bridge methods into such an internal class rather than exposing them on the stable entrypoint.

threads.body:
`capture(endpoint, command)` here passes the `DefaultEndpoint` instance as the batch-state key, but `LettuceBatchSupport.batchStates` is only ever populated by `setAutoFlushCommands(commands, ...)`, whose key is the `AbstractRedisAsyncCommands` instance (`SetAutoFlushAdvice` matches `io.lettuce.core.AbstractRedisAsyncCommands`). Since the `DefaultEndpoint` is never registered as a key, `batchStates.get(endpoint)` is always `null` and this capture is a no-op, making `LettuceDefaultEndpointInstrumentation` effectively dead.

Every command is already captured via `LettuceAsyncCommandsInstrumentation.DispatchAdvice` (which keys on the same `AbstractRedisAsyncCommands` instance as `setAutoFlushCommands`), so this instrumentation appears redundant and can likely be removed (along with its registration in `LettuceInstrumentationModule`). If it was instead intended to capture commands written through a path that bypasses `dispatch`, the endpoint would need to be registered as its own batch-state key — but note that keying it the same as `dispatch` would double-count commands.

threads.body:
The batch span's error is taken only from the throwable of whichever command completes last (the call that decrements `remaining` to 0). Because `endOne` is invoked once per command completion via `handleAsync`, and Redis command errors are per-command, an earlier command in the pipeline can complete exceptionally while the last command succeeds. In that case the earlier failure is silently dropped and the aggregate batch span is recorded as successful.

The sibling lettuce-5.1 implementation handles this by accumulating the first non-null error across all commands (`BatchScope.finishOne` in `OpenTelemetryTracing`). Consider accumulating the error here as well (e.g. store the first non-null throwable in a field and pass it at `end`), so failures from non-last commands aren't lost.

threads.body: `startCommand` runs for every Redis command (it is invoked from the newly instrumented `CommandHandler.writeSingleCommand`), and the companion `capture` runs for every `DefaultEndpoint.write`. Both perform lookups against the global `Collections.synchronizedMap(WeakHashMap)` instances (`activeBatchCommands` here, `writerBatchStates`'s inner map in `capture`). This monitor acquisition is paid on the command hot path even when deferred flush is never used, so under high-throughput, multi-threaded workloads these shared monitors can become a contention point that serializes command writes across connections. Consider a cheap fast path — e.g. a `volatile` counter/flag tracking whether any batch is currently active — so `startCommand`/`capture` can return immediately without touching the synchronized maps when no batch state exists. This is optional; the impact is typically small relative to Redis I/O.

replies.body: Good call. Replaced the `Collections.synchronizedMap(WeakHashMap)` lookups with `VirtualField` (per-connection and per-command state), so `startCommand`/`capture` are now lock-free per-object reads with no shared monitor on the command hot path. While doing this I also flipped the module dependency: the `VirtualField`-backed implementation now lives in the javaagent module behind a new `LettuceBatching` SPI seam in the library, so the library no longer references agent-only APIs. Fixed in d308a02742e6001fb0017ccfacb397f96d179579.

threads.body: what are pros and cons to having 2 getters (one for reg and one for batch)?

replies.body: Keeping the two getters. They're parameterized on different request types (`RedisCommand` for per-command spans, the precomputed `LettuceBatchRequest` snapshot for batch spans), and one class can't implement `DbClientAttributesGetter` for both; the batch getter also supplies `getDbOperationBatchSize`. Unifying into one request type is feasible but would force wrapping every single command in a request object (extra allocation + eager operationName/queryText compute) on the hot path, purely to satisfy the batch snapshot — which exists only because the command list is cleared at flush. The only shared code is a couple of trivial constant methods, so the duplication isn't worth that cost.
